title: Breaking the color line; the Beachcomber on Pearl Harbor day
summary: Latin bands were white, he says; he subs at the Beachcomber on December 7, 1941.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I said, well, the young generation began to like Machido, because they never heard nothing like that, and they were familiar to them because they were born here, and the sound is familiar to them, and they really (inaudible). So (inaudible) nobody else. The Latin band that was here was a hinky-dinky band.
First, nobody predicted this band will go, because it was the color line too. Latin bands in those days here were pure white. To play in the Stork Club, the Morocco, the Rhumba

Room, all right, I didn't worry about it. I was going to break that line. That ain't nothing I worried about. Music was going to break that. So I proved it. About six months after the band, no, five months after the band was already started, which I got call to go in there and work couple week as a substitute in The Beachcomber nightclub, over there on Broadway where the Waikiki is today.
That would be '41. I never forget. The day the Pearl Harber, December 7 -- Pearl Harbor?

We was playing matinee in that club that afternoon when that thing came (inaudible). So the musicians, they had nothing to say. They know -- they knew my music was so ahead of time for them, they wouldn't know even reason to talk about.

The (inaudible) you know, here and want that there, you know, and all that. They ain't going to be able to play those shows. Well, after the show I play (inaudible). So we work in there the two weeks or whatever. We finish there. We go back to the barrio and play more than (inaudible) JACK Harris. He's a violin player. He's the owner. He used to have a big club in London. He's a big man club, a nightclub man. He's a violin player, had his own band there.
